details:
**Sabina's bowler hat**
Sabina is a Czech painter and Tomas's mistress. She wears a black bowler hat, often with nothing else on, during sex with Tomas and later with Franz. The hat belonged to her grandfather, and when her father died it was the only thing she wanted to inherit. Tereza also photographs her wearing it.

**"War on kitsch"**
Sabina declares war on kitsch, which the novel defines as an aesthetic ideal that denies the existence of shit and hides everything ugly about human life. She especially hates the "totalitarian kitsch" of Communist May Day parades. The novel's discussion of kitsch begins with Stalin's son Yakov, who died by throwing himself against an electric fence in a POW camp, and with the question of whether God has intestines.

**Tomas's Oedipus article**
Tomas, a gifted Prague surgeon, writes a letter to a newspaper comparing the Czech Communists to Oedipus. Oedipus blinded himself when he learned what he had done unknowingly, so Tomas argues that Communists who say they "didn't know" should still take responsibility. After the Soviet invasion, the Chief Surgeon and the authorities pressure him to sign a statement retracting it, and he refuses more than once.

**Tomas becomes a window washer**
Because he refuses to retract the article, Tomas can no longer work as a surgeon. He first works as a country doctor and then becomes a window washer in Prague. The job gives him more chances to seduce women.

**Karenin**
Karenin is Tomas and Tereza's dog. She is female but has a male name, taken from Anna Karenina's husband in Tolstoy's novel. On the collective farm she befriends a pig named Mefisto. She dies of a cancerous tumor on her leg after Tomas puts her down with an injection, and the novel's final part is called "Karenin's Smile."

**"Es muss sein!"**
This German phrase means "It must be!" It comes from the last movement of Beethoven's final string quartet (Op. 135), where it answers the question "Muss es sein?" ("Must it be?"). Tomas uses it to stand for necessity and fate. He says it to his boss in Zurich when he quits his job to follow Tereza back to occupied Prague, and he wonders whether his love for Tereza is his own "es muss sein."

**Franz and the Grand March in Cambodia**
Franz is a married Swiss professor in Geneva who becomes Sabina's lover. Longing to be part of the "Grand March" of history, he joins a protest march of Western intellectuals and celebrities to the Cambodian border, where they are turned back. An American actress bursts into tears during the march after being insulted. Soon afterward Franz is beaten by muggers in Bangkok and dies from his injuries.

**"A return after long wanderings"**
Franz's wife, Marie-Claude, has this inscription put on his gravestone. She takes charge of his body and treats his affair with a young student as a midlife crisis, imagining that he came back to her begging for forgiveness. The novel mocks her as the "Platonic ideal of a woman," and she declares that "Stendhal is a night author!"

**"He wanted the Kingdom of God on Earth"**
Simon, Tomas's estranged son from an earlier marriage, has this epitaph put on his father's grave. Simon is religious, and he is also the one who writes to Sabina to tell her that Tomas and Tereza have died.

**Death of Tomas and Tereza in a truck accident**
After moving to a collective farm in the countryside, Tomas and Tereza are killed when the brakes of their truck fail and they are crushed underneath it. The novel reveals their deaths early, through Simon's letter to Sabina, who then moves to California.

**Eternal return and "Einmal ist keinmal"**
The novel opens with Nietzsche's idea of eternal return, the idea that everything recurs endlessly, which would give life "weight." It contrasts this with Parmenides's division of the world into opposites, including lightness and heaviness, and asks whether heaviness is truly deplorable and lightness splendid. The German saying "Einmal ist keinmal" ("What happens once might as well not have happened at all") sums up the lightness of a life lived only once. Italo Calvino praises this quality of the novel in "Lightness," the first of his Six Memos for the Next Millennium.

**Tereza's photography**
Tereza first works as a waitress in a provincial town, where six coincidences ("fortuities") bring her and Tomas together, including Beethoven playing in the restaurant. In Prague, Sabina helps her move from the darkroom to working as a photographer. Tereza photographs the Soviet invasion of 1968, and she later worries that the police used her photos to identify protesters.

**"Dictionary of Misunderstood Words"**
This section of the novel defines words such as "woman," "music," and "cemetery." Each word means something different to Sabina and Franz, which shows why the two lovers cannot understand each other. It contains the line "if you're looking for infinity, just close your eyes."

**"He gave birth to two rolls and a bee"**
This is the inscription on Karenin's grave. It refers to Tereza's dream in which Karenin gives birth to two rolls (bread) and a bee.

**Tomas's "erotic friendships"**
Tomas is a compulsive womanizer who has slept with around two hundred women. He keeps his mistresses as "erotic friends" and claims his affairs do not change his love for his wife, Tereza. The novel calls him an "epic" rather than "lyrical" womanizer, and he searches each woman for the "one-millionth part" that makes her unique, which he believes appears only in bed.
